issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette:
Ethan's Story

Ethan Parata was twenty-four when his older brother Kai died. It happened on a Friday night in March, two years ago, though the specific sequence of events still refuses to arrange itself into a coherent narrative in Ethan's mind. He knows that Kai had been drinking at a friend's house. He knows that Kai drove. He knows that somewhere on the Pacific Coast Highway, Kai's car crossed the median. He knows his mother called him at midnight. Beyond those anchors, the story fragments—pieces that won't fit together, gaps he cannot fill even when he tries to reconstruct it deliberately. Sometimes he remembers the hospital waiting room; sometimes he remembers his father's face. But he cannot hold the whole thing in his mind at once, cannot tell it as a beginning, middle, and end. It is only a series of moments that happened to someone else, to a version of Ethan who no longer exists.

Kai had always been the golden one. Three years older, confident, the kind of person who made friends easily and seemed to know instinctively how to live. Ethan had followed him into pharmacy school—not because he wanted to, he realized later, but because Kai had made it seem possible, achievable, normal. In the weeks after Kai's death, Ethan found himself unable to sit in the pharmacy where he now worked without feeling the weight of that mimicry, that false inheritance of Kai's certainty. He had come to believe that his life was destroyed, that he had been following a path that was never truly his, that the person he had been before—the one who could laugh, who had felt purposeful in his work—had died along with Kai.

The smell of alcohol undoes him. It arrives without warning: a customer at the pharmacy who has been drinking, a colleague's breath, the sharp tang of hand sanitizer on a particularly bad day. His body reacts before his mind has time to register what is happening. His chest tightens. His hands shake. He becomes hypervigilant, scanning the pharmacy for danger that he knows, intellectually, is not there. He has come to understand that his body is constantly braced, as if waiting for another catastrophe, as if remaining vigilant enough might somehow prevent what has already happened. At night, he lies awake, muscles tense, certain that something terrible is about to occur, only to wake to the ordinary silence of his apartment.

Ethan has begun avoiding situations where he might encounter people behaving recklessly or selfishly. He stopped attending his weekly soccer league because of a player who had shown up late and dismissive of the team's rules. The violation—the disregard for others, the carelessness—triggered something in him that felt like rage and terror combined. He finds himself judging people harshly, withdrawing from friends who drink, creating distance from anyone whose behavior seems to him morally compromised. When he recalls Kai's decision to drive that night, the guilt is suffocating. Kai was reckless. Kai made a choice. And Ethan cannot separate his grief from his anger at that choice, cannot hold both feelings without feeling like he is betraying his brother.

When his mother invited him to a cemetery dedication last month—a small gathering to mark Kai's grave with a new stone—Ethan's body seized with panic before his mind could process the invitation. He could not go. The thought of standing in that space, surrounded by the physical reality of his brother's death, surrounded by his family's grief, felt impossible. He declined. His mother has not called since.

It is this avoidance, this shrinking away from the world, that finally brought Ethan to his first therapy appointment. He is twenty-six now, and he realizes that he has spent the last two years becoming smaller—smaller in his job, smaller in his relationships, smaller in his own life. He came seeking help not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is afraid that if he continues as he is, there will be nothing left of him at all. What he fears most is that this is permanent, that the person he was before Kai died is truly gone. What he hopes for, though he barely dares to articulate it, is some way to live alongside the grief without being consumed by it.
